title: Domain-specific institutional trust aligns with retirement behavior differently across groups
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 35220; Health and Retirement Study trust module and older U.S. households
geography: United States; older households observed in the Health and Retirement Study

observations.period: Health and Retirement Study trust and retirement-security measures; 2026 working paper

denominator.unit: HRS respondents with outcome-specific trust, financial-literacy, and retirement-security measures; common analytic count not disclosed in the abstract

financial_institution_trust.value: Trust in financial institutions aligns positively with behaviors supportive of retirement security

government_program_trust.value: Trust in government programs does not show the same positive alignment and is negatively linked to selected wealth behaviors

financial_literacy.value: Financial literacy is also associated with retirement-security behaviors

observations.method: HRS observational analysis relating newly measured trust domains and financial literacy to retirement-account ownership, stockholding, and household net wealth; estimates distinguish financial-institution trust from government-program trust.
observations.uncertainty: Associations do not establish that trust caused saving, stockholding, or wealth. Reverse causality, selection, prior experiences, financial access, and unmeasured resources may shape both trust and outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Older U.S. households in the HRS; outcomes and relationships vary by trust domain and racial/ethnic group.
observations.counterinterpretation: People with greater resources or better financial access may trust institutions more, rather than trust itself producing the observed behavior. Institutional trust may also reflect prior outcomes.

denominator.unit: HRS racial/ethnic subgroups with outcome-specific observations; subgroup counts not disclosed in the public abstract

white_respondents.value: Financial-institution trust is positively related to retirement outcomes for White respondents

black_hispanic_respondents.value: The same positive relationship is not observed in the same form for Black or Hispanic respondents

minority_government_trust.value: Trust in government programs among minority households is linked to reduced stockholding and lower wealth accumulation

observations.method: Subgroup analysis of the HRS trust and retirement-security measures, distinguishing racial/ethnic patterns and the domain of institutional trust.
observations.uncertainty: The abstract does not provide all subgroup denominators or specification details; the contrasts are not proof of a single mechanism such as discrimination, access, or institutional experience.
observations.subgroup: White, Black, and Hispanic older U.S. households; subgroup estimates should not be collapsed into a universal trust effect.
observations.counterinterpretation: Differences may reflect wealth, account access, cohort, health, financial advice, prior institutional treatment, or measurement differences rather than trust alone.

related_sources.claim: The Bank of Israel hosts the accessible paper version and abstract.
The HRS publication record identifies the paper and its HRS-based research context.

boundary: This record adds an observed trust-to-financial-behavior bridge in older U.S. households, with domain and racial/ethnic heterogeneity. It does not establish causal trust effects, current working-age behavior, retirement adequacy, institutional legitimacy, political action, or why the associations differ. Trust, financial access, behavior, wealth, and durable security remain separate stages.
